clue.text: Gobbled up five-nil by the City, indeed !

indicators.note: the word indeed splits into in plus deed, so the first half tells us the rest goes inside

parts.note: deed is taken as written from the second half of indeed
V is the Roman numeral for five
nil is zero, which looks like the letter O
Ur is the ancient Mesopotamian city, a crossword favourite

explanation.surface: A football fan crows that the City side was thrashed five-nil.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Indeed' must be split as 'in deed', with 'in' as the container signal. 'Five-nil' and 'City' read as a football score; 'by' is only a link.
explanation.definitionFit: To devour food is to eat it greedily, which is what gobbling means.

clue.text: What people put down is back in the bus sheds

indicators.note: in tells us the turned short word sits inside the garage word

parts.note: depots are garages where buses are kept

indicators.note: back means the word is is read the other way round

explanation.surface: Something people leave behind turns up in the bus garages.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Back' reverses only the little word 'is'; bus sheds are the garages buses are kept in.
explanation.definitionFit: Money paid down as security, or sediment laid down, are both things put down.

clue.text: Leo chasing tail-less mice, say, in colour

indicators.note: chasing means coming after, so the star-sign word follows
tail-less means the word loses its final letter

parts.note: mice are an example of vermin, which the say flags
Leo is the lion of the zodiac

explanation.surface: A big cat pursues mice that have lost their tails, in vivid colour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tail-less' drops the last letter of the vermin word and 'chasing' puts the lion after it. Leo looks like a name but is the zodiac lion.
explanation.definitionFit: Vermilion is a brilliant scarlet pigment, so it is a colour.

clue.text: Such impulses may cause surge

indicators.note: may cause means the letters of the last word are rearranged to produce the answer

explanation.surface: Strong impulses may trigger a rush of feeling.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer's letters rearranged make SURGE; 'such' points the definition at the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Urges are sudden strong desires, which is what impulses are.

clue.text: Lets the girl in 26 take a note to a boy

parts.note: Ena is a girl's name sitting inside the answer at 26 across
B is a note in the musical scale
Les is a boy's name, short for Leslie

explanation.surface: A girl takes a message to a boy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The girl in 26' is ENA, found inside MENAI at 26 across; 'take' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: To enable someone is to allow or permit them, which is to let them.

clue.text: A loud blonde may have one

definitions.text: A loud blonde may have one

parts.note: F stands for forte, the musical marking for loud
fair hair is blonde hair

explanation.surface: A brash fair-haired woman is the type gossip pins a liaison on.
explanation.walkthrough: A, F (forte) and FAIR spell the answer, and the whole clue hints that such a woman might have one: the setter plays on a stock caricature.
explanation.definitionFit: A love affair is the romantic entanglement the gossip in the clue imagines.

clue.text: Warning device, the genuine article in business

indicators.note: in tells us the adjective and article sit inside the company word

parts.note: a firm is a business
real means genuine
a is the indefinite article

explanation.surface: An authentic warning bell is installed in the office.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The genuine article' reads as one phrase but splits into REAL and A; 'the' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A fire alarm is a bell or siren that warns of fire.

clue.text: A stone may bar the way

explanation.surface: A stone might block the path.
explanation.definitionFit: Agate is a banded chalcedony gemstone, and a gate is what stands across a path to bar it.

clue.text: In turn, consumed, with decay

indicators.note: with joins the two pieces, the decay word coming first in the answer

parts.note: rot is decay
ate means consumed

explanation.surface: Food eaten in sequence goes off.
explanation.definitionFit: To rotate duties is to take them by turns, one after another.

clue.text: Evermore ——, the exchequer of the poor" (Richard II)

definitions.text: Evermore ——, the exchequer of the poor" (Richard II)

parts.words: Evermore ——, the exchequer of the poor" (Richard II)
parts.note: a fill-in: the missing word from Bolingbroke's line in Shakespeare's Richard II

explanation.surface: A line from Shakespeare's history play with a word missing.
explanation.walkthrough: In Richard II, Act 2 Scene 3, Bolingbroke says gratitude is all the poor can pay: 'Evermore thanks, the exchequer of the poor.'
explanation.definitionFit: Gratitude expressed in words costs nothing, so it is the only payment the poor can make.

clue.text: Some writing may be of equal value to a symbolic diagram

parts.note: at par means of equal value, as with shares or currencies
a graph is a diagram showing data in symbolic form

explanation.surface: Someone muses that a passage of text may be worth as much as a chart.
explanation.walkthrough: 'May be' and 'to' are link words joining the definition to the pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: A paragraph is a block of prose, so it is a piece of writing.

clue.text: A sort of a sort of joint

indicators.note: of here means made of, so the letters of the opening words are made into something new

explanation.surface: A dithering phrase, a sort of a sort of, as if the speaker cannot name the cut of meat.
explanation.walkthrough: The repetition looks like stammering, but the first 'A sort' is the anagram fodder and the second 'a sort of joint' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A Sunday roast is a cut of meat cooked in the oven, a kind of joint.

clue.text: Frisks quietly in slippers

indicators.note: in tells us the soft-music letter sits inside the footwear word

parts.note: skis are things one slips along on, hence slippers
P stands for piano, the musical marking for quietly

explanation.surface: Someone gambols softly about the house in bedroom slippers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Slippers' looks like house shoes, but here it means skis, things that slip over snow.
explanation.definitionFit: To frisk is to leap playfully, and skipping is that kind of lively hopping.

clue.text: Feature one point in the elegy

indicators.note: in signals that the number and compass letters go inside the mourning poem

parts.note: an elegy is a lament, a poem of mourning
I is the Roman numeral for one
NE, north-east, is a point of the compass

explanation.surface: A critic praises one moment in a mournful poem as its standout feature.
explanation.definitionFit: Lineaments are the distinctive outlines of a face, its characteristic features.

clue.text: A girl falls amongst this-or these ?

indicators.note: falls amongst means drops into the middle of, so the woman's name goes inside

parts.note: this is taken as written
Eve is a girl's name, the first woman in Genesis

explanation.surface: The Good Samaritan parable, where a traveller fell among thieves, is invoked with a girl as victim.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase recalls the man who 'fell among thieves' in Luke's parable, so the definition 'these' is the very word the phrase supplies.
explanation.definitionFit: These points back to the people a traveller falls among in the parable: robbers.

clue.text: A change of theme ?

parts.note: theme in its musical sense: a composer reworking a melody produces a set of these

explanation.surface: Someone switches topic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Theme' suggests a subject of talk, but in music a theme is altered in a set of pieces bearing this name.
explanation.definitionFit: A musical variation is a modified version of a theme, so it changes it.

clue.text: They are impressive, even when made of rubber

definitions.text: They are impressive, even when made of rubber

parts.words: They are impressive, even when made of rubber
parts.note: impressive means making an impression, as an inked device pressed on paper does; office ones are often rubber

explanation.surface: Praise for things that impress even though they are only made of rubber.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Impressive' looks like praise but means 'leaving an impression', as a rubber stamp does on paper.
explanation.definitionFit: Rubber stamps press an inked mark onto paper, literally making impressions.

clue.text: Booked with pride

parts.note: booked with means paired in a book title; Jane Austen's novel title joins pride to one more noun

explanation.surface: Someone made a reservation, proudly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Booked' suggests a reservation, but it means joined in a book's title: Jane Austen's 'Pride and Prejudice'.
explanation.definitionFit: Austen's 1813 novel pairs pride with bias in its title.

clue.text: "I often wonder what the buy " (Fitzgerald)

parts.note: a fill-in from Edward FitzGerald's Rubaiyat of Omar Khayyam: the missing word names wine sellers

explanation.surface: A line from FitzGerald's Rubaiyat with a word missing.
explanation.walkthrough: FitzGerald's Rubaiyat ends the quatrain 'I often wonder what the Vintners buy / One half so precious as the stuff they sell.' The OCR dropped the dash for the gap.
explanation.definitionFit: Wine merchants sell wine, which the poem rates above anything they could buy.

clue.text: Twists beastly aggressive remarks

explanation.surface: Someone spins and growls angry comments like an animal.
explanation.definitionFit: Tangles in rope are knots called by the same word, and a dog's growls with bared teeth give the second sense.

clue.text: Tremble a tiny bit

explanation.surface: Someone quakes slightly.
explanation.definitionFit: To quiver with cold is to tremble, and a splinter or sliver of glass is a tiny fragment.

clue.text: City brings splendid display to Wanstead district

parts.note: pomp is splendid ceremonial display
Wanstead is in the London postal district E11, written here with the 1s as Is

explanation.surface: A town puts on a grand parade for an area of east London.
explanation.walkthrough: Wanstead is a district of east London whose postcode is E11; the ones are read as the letter I.
explanation.definitionFit: The Roman city buried by Vesuvius in AD 79 is a famous ancient city.

clue.text: Bridge is a card game

explanation.surface: The card game bridge is described as a card game.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bridge' looks like the card game, which matches the second definition, but here it is a floating bridge on boats; 'is' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A floating bridge rests on flat-bottomed boats, and vingt-et-un is also known by the same name.

clue.text: Licence needed for every thousand, it appears

parts.note: per means for each, as in per head
M is the Roman numeral for a thousand

explanation.surface: A permit seems to be required for each thousand.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Needed' and 'appears' are link words.
explanation.definitionFit: A permit is an official document of authorisation, which is what a licence is.

clue.text: No TV authority call brought back this issue

indicators.note: brought back means the whole run of pieces is read from the end to the start

parts.note: the ITA was the Independent Television Authority, which ran UK commercial TV until 1972
to call someone something is to name them

explanation.surface: A broadcasting regulator declines to recall a programme.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Brought back' turns NO + ITA + NAME into EMAN + ATI + ON. The ITA was Britain's commercial television regulator at the time; 'this' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: An emanation is something that flows out from a source, an issue in the sense of outflow.

clue.text: Girl and boy record

parts.note: Ann is a girl's name
Al is a boy's name, short for Alan or Albert

explanation.surface: A boy and a girl set down an account.
explanation.definitionFit: An annal is a yearly chronicle entry, a historical record.

clue.text: One with will-power can create such confidence

definitions.text: One with will-power can create such confidence

parts.words: One with will-power can create such confidence
parts.note: will-power reads as the power given by a legal will, which can set up a fund held for others; the word also means confidence

explanation.surface: A determined person can inspire faith in others.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Will-power' looks like determination, but means the power of a legal will, which can create a fund held by trustees.
explanation.definitionFit: Confidence in someone is faith in them, and a legal fund set up by a will shares the same word.

clue.text: Some cavalry turning left round the circle

indicators.note: round says the reversed side word wraps the ring letter
turning means the word for left is read back to front

parts.note: port is the left side of a ship
a circle is shaped like the letter O

explanation.surface: A cavalry squadron wheels left around the ring.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turning' makes PORT into TROP, and O goes inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: A troop is a cavalry unit, a number of horsemen.

clue.text: Implying that : women are second-rate at bridge ?

definitions.text: Implying that : women are second-rate at bridge ?

parts.words: Implying that : women are second-rate at bridge ?
parts.note: split the bridge's name into a word for males plus the grade for first-rate: if the males are top grade, women by implication come second

explanation.surface: A sexist suggestion that women play poorly at the card game bridge.
explanation.walkthrough: Bridge suggests the card game, but it is Telford's suspension bridge in north Wales. Split the name into males plus the top grade (A1), which implies women come second.
explanation.definitionFit: The Menai Bridge spans the Menai Strait between mainland Wales and Anglesey.

clue.text: Is one come to ruin from failure to do so ?

definitions.text: Is one come to ruin from failure to do so ?

indicators.note: to ruin means to wreck, so the opening three words are broken up and rebuilt

explanation.surface: A rueful question: is someone bankrupt because they never cut back?
explanation.walkthrough: The anagram of IS ONE COME gives the answer, and the whole question also hints at it: ruin follows a failure to save.
explanation.definitionFit: Failing to cut spending is the usual route to financial ruin.

clue.text: Ability to have a drink in explosive surroundings

indicators.note: surroundings says the explosive letters wrap round the beer

parts.note: TNT, trinitrotoluene, is the standard explosive
ale is a drink, a kind of beer

explanation.surface: Someone boasts of a knack for drinking amid explosions.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' is a link; 'surroundings' is the container signal, the explosive wrapping the beer.
explanation.definitionFit: Talent is natural skill or aptitude, so it is a kind of ability.

clue.text: Poodle parlour activity may produce these

definitions.text: Poodle parlour activity may produce these

parts.words: Poodle parlour activity may produce these
parts.note: the work done in a dog-grooming salon reads as cutting pets, giving clippings or scraps

explanation.surface: Trimmings left over in a dog-grooming salon.
explanation.walkthrough: A poodle parlour is a dog-grooming salon; split the answer as SNIP PETS, what the groomers do.
explanation.definitionFit: Small cut-off scraps or fragments are what clipping fur produces.
